s: Good morning, Riverside Fitness. How can I help? Hello, I'd like to join the gym. Certainly. Are you a student? Yes, I'm at the university. Then you can have the student rate, which is thirty-five pounds a month instead of forty-five. There is also a joining fee of twenty pounds, but it is free if you sign up before the end of March. Can I use the swimming pool? Yes, the pool is included, but classes such as yoga cost an extra five pounds each. The gym opens at six in the morning and closes at ten at night on weekdays, and at eight in the evening at weekends. Great. I'll come in on Thursday afternoon to sign the form. Please bring your student card and a form of photo identification.

s: Welcome to the accommodation office. We have three types of room. The first is a single room in a shared flat, which costs one hundred and twenty pounds a week. The second is a studio with its own kitchen and bathroom, which costs one hundred and eighty. The third is a twin room, shared with another student, at ninety pounds each. Applications must be in by the fifteenth of June, and you will hear the result within ten days. A deposit equal to two weeks' rent is due after you accept.

s: Welcome, everyone, to your library induction. I'll be quick, because I know you want to start exploring. The ground floor is for group work, and talking is fine there. The first floor is a quiet zone, so please keep your voices low. On the second floor you will find silent study rooms, which you can book online for up to three hours. The books are arranged by subject number, not by author, so ask at the desk if you cannot find something. You may borrow ten books at a time for four weeks. If you keep a book longer, the fine is fifty pence a day. Printing is on the ground floor, and you need to add credit to your card first. Finally, the library closes at midnight during exams, but it is only open until eight in the evening on Sundays.

s: Good afternoon and welcome to the Heritage Museum. We'll begin in the entrance hall, where you can see a model of the town as it was in eighteen hundred. Then we move to the east wing, which tells the story of the local textile industry. Please do not touch the machines, even though they look sturdy. After that, we'll go upstairs to the photography gallery, which has been closed for repairs but reopened last week. The café is next to the gift shop, and it offers a ten per cent discount to anyone with a tour ticket. The tour lasts about ninety minutes, and there is a short break halfway. Photography is allowed everywhere except in the gallery, where flash damages the old prints. Please stay with the group, because some rooms are locked after the tour passes.

s: Tutor: So, Dilnoza, tell me about your project on urban beekeeping. Dilnoza: Well, I assumed bees would struggle in cities, but the research suggests the opposite. City bees often produce more honey than rural ones, because gardens and parks flower for longer. Tutor: Interesting. What problems did you find? Dilnoza: Mainly competition. In some cities there are now so many hives that wild bees have less food. Tutor: So the hives may actually harm wild species? Dilnoza: Possibly, yes. That is the part I'm still unsure about, because the evidence is mixed. Tutor: Then I'd suggest presenting both views fairly, and not just defending beekeeping. Also, check your sources, because one of your statistics came from a company that sells hives. Dilnoza: Good point. I'll look for independent studies.

q.q: What did Dilnoza expect at first?
Why do city bees often make more honey?
What is the main problem she found?
o: Competition for food with wild bees

q.q: How does Dilnoza feel about the evidence?
What does the tutor warn her about?
o: A source from a company selling hives

s: Tutor: You have chosen interviews for your study of student sleep. Why not a questionnaire? Student: A questionnaire would give me more responses, but the answers would be shallow. I want people to explain their habits. Tutor: That's reasonable, though interviews take much longer. How many do you plan to do? Student: About twelve, each of thirty minutes. Tutor: Twelve is fine for a small project. But what about bias? People might say they sleep more than they really do. Student: That is a risk. I could ask them to keep a sleep diary for a week as well, and compare it with what they say. Tutor: That is a good solution. Just remember that you need their written consent, and you must keep their names anonymous.

q.q: Why does the student prefer interviews?
What is the drawback of interviews?
o: They give fewer answers than expected

q.q: How many interviews are planned?
How will the student reduce bias?
o: Use a sleep diary for a week

q.q: What must the student obtain?

s: Today I'd like to talk about the early history of the bicycle. The first machine of this kind, built in the early nineteenth century, had no pedals at all. Riders pushed along with their feet, so it was more like a scooter with a seat. Pedals appeared on the front wheel in the eighteen sixties, and these machines were called boneshakers because of their wooden wheels. Later, the front wheel was made very large to increase speed, but this design was dangerous, as riders fell from a great height. The breakthrough came with the safety bicycle in the eighteen eighties, which had two wheels of equal size and a chain driving the back wheel. Rubber tyres filled with air soon made riding far more comfortable. Within a decade, bicycles had become popular with ordinary people, and many historians argue that they helped women gain greater independence.

q.q: What was unusual about the first machine?
Why were the pedal machines called boneshakers?
What was the problem with the huge front wheel?
What made the safety bicycle different?
o: Two wheels of equal size and a chain

q.q: What do many historians say about bicycles?

s: Scientists have long debated why we dream. One theory says that dreams help the brain sort the day's memories, strengthening the important ones and discarding the rest. A second theory claims that dreaming is a kind of rehearsal for danger, which would explain why so many dreams involve being chased. A third idea is more modest: dreams may simply be a by-product of brain activity during sleep, with no purpose at all. Evidence for the first theory comes from experiments in which people who learned a new task and then slept performed better the next day. However, these results do not prove that dreams were responsible, since deep sleep may be the real cause. Researchers agree on one point: people who are deprived of the dreaming stage of sleep tend to become irritable and forgetful.

q.q: What does the first theory say dreams do?
What does the second theory explain?
o: Why many dreams involve being chased

q.q: What does the third idea suggest?
o: Dreams are a by-product with no purpose

q.q: Why do the experiments not prove the first theory?
o: Deep sleep might be the real cause

q.q: What happens to people deprived of dreaming sleep?

s: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they support about a quarter of all marine species. This is why scientists often call them the rainforests of the sea. Corals are tiny animals that live in partnership with algae. The algae give the coral its colour and supply food through photosynthesis. When the water becomes too warm, the coral expels the algae, turns white and may die. This process, called bleaching, has become more common in recent decades. Other threats include pollution from farms, which encourages harmful algae to grow, and damage from boat anchors. On a positive note, some reefs have recovered when fishing was restricted and water quality improved. Scientists are also growing corals in nurseries and transplanting them to damaged areas, although this is expensive and cannot yet be done on a large scale.

q.q: What proportion of the ocean floor do reefs cover?
What do the algae provide for the coral?
What causes bleaching?
How does farm pollution harm reefs?
Why is transplanting coral limited?
o: It is expensive and cannot be done at scale
